Project Summary: LunarSight

LunarSight is an open-source, full-stack scientific visualization and mission-planning platform dedicated to the lunar south pole (80°S to 90°S). Designed for aerospace engineers, researchers, students, and space enthusiasts, LunarSight enables interactive exploration of lunar topography, scientific assessment of NASA Artemis candidate landing regions, and precise modeling of solar illumination and Earth line-of-sight availability using authentic NASA mission data.

1. What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

LunarSight integrates high-resolution lunar orbital datasets with space ephemeris engines into a cohesive web system:

  • Interactive 3D Lunar Globe: Built with Three.js and React Three Fiber, users can freely rotate the Moon in any direction across its poles, inspect candidate landing regions with zoom-adaptive markers, and explore surface relief.
  • Cartographic 2D Scientific Maps: Renders 2D polar stereographic projections (IAU2015:30135) of NASA LOLA digital elevation models (DEM), computing real-time layers for topographic elevation, Horn’s slope gradient, surface RMS roughness, and 36-azimuth horizon-shadowed solar illumination.
  • Terrain-Aware Ephemeris & Solar Analysis: Powered by NASA NAIF SPICE kernels, users select any custom lunar coordinates, start epoch, and date range. The system computes exact solar elevation/azimuth vectors and runs a 360-degree ray-cast over local LOLA DEM topography (accounting for lunar spherical curvature) to determine whether the Sun is blocked by crater rims or peaks.
  • Earth Visibility & Communication Geometry: Computes Earth elevation and range over time, providing line-of-sight visibility windows for direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication planning.
  • Interactive 2D Sun–Moon–Earth Geometric Model: Translates multi-body celestial coordinates into an intuitive, time-scrubbable 2D elevation model featuring the Sun, Moon terminator shading, and Earth.
  • Candidate Region Trade Studies: Enables side-by-side quantitative comparisons across the 13 published NASA Artemis III south pole candidate regions.

2. What Benefits and Intended Impact Does It Have?

  • Eliminates Scientific Placeholders: Many lunar outreach tools rely on synthetic terrain or placeholder numbers. LunarSight processes actual NASA elevation GeoTIFFs and JPL ephemeris kernels on the fly, delivering authentic science.
  • Accelerates Mission Planning & Education: Users can quickly identify optimal landing zones by trading off landing hazard risks (slope and roughness) against solar power longevity and direct-to-Earth communication access.
  • Promotes Data Accessibility: Complex planetary data (SPICE kernels, 16-bit PDS GeoTIFFs) is transformed into an intuitive, browser-accessible interface requiring zero local software installation.

3. Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

  • Backend Architecture:
    • Python & FastAPI: High-performance RESTful scientific API service.
    • SpiceyPy: C-wrapper for the NASA NAIF SPICE toolkit for celestial mechanics and ephemerides.
    • Rasterio & GDAL: Geospatial raster manipulation and GeoTIFF reading.
    • PyProj / PROJ: Precise coordinate reference transformations between lunar body-fixed selenographic coordinates and polar stereographic planes.
    • NumPy & SciPy: Gradient calculations, windowed spatial filtering, and vector trigonometry.
  • Frontend Architecture:
    • React & Vite: Fast client-side single-page application.
    • Three.js, React Three Fiber & Drei: WebGL 3D rendering engine for the interactive lunar globe.
    • Plotly.js: Scientific heatmap and interactive time-series charting.
    • IBM Plex Typography & CSS Variables: High-contrast scientific UI design system adhering to strict readability guidelines.
  • Authoritative NASA Datasets:
    • NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) DEMs (PGDA Product 78 & SVS 4720).
    • NASA NAIF SPICE Kernels (de440s.bsp, pck00011.tpc, naif0012.tls).
    • NASA Exploration Systems Development Directorate Artemis III Candidate Regions.
    • NASA CGI Moon Kit (SVS 14959) & LROC WAC Global Relief Basemaps.

4. How Is the Project Creative and Innovative?

  • Dual Visual/Quantitative Exploration: Combines a fluid, free-rotation 3D globe with analytical 2D cartographic rasters and orbital models, letting users switch between macro-scale context and micro-scale landing-site inspection.
  • Curvature-Corrected Horizon Ray-Casting: Rather than simply checking whether the Sun is above 0°, the platform dynamically shoots 72 to 360 radial rays up to 50 km across the LOLA elevation grid, factoring in lunar radius curvature (Δh=d2/(2RMoon)\Delta h = d^2 / (2 R_{\text{Moon}})Δh=d2/(2RMoon​)) to compute true topographic shadow masks.
  • Dynamic 2D Orbital Scrubbing: The dedicated 2D Sun–Moon–Earth model provides an intuitive, animated cross-section of celestial positions relative to the astronaut's local horizon.

5. What Critical Factors Did the Team Consider?

  • Scientific Honesty & Rigor: Clearly distinguishes geometric line-of-sight from terrain-shadowed visibility. It explicitly labels Earth visibility as geometric/topographic line-of-sight rather than a guaranteed RF link budget, educating users on the difference between unobstructed views and RF link margins.
  • Resolution vs. Pixel Spacing: Accurately documents that grid spacing (e.g., 1000 m/px) is distinct from effective terrain resolution.
  • No Hardcoded Values: All slopes, roughness metrics, solar elevation curves, and illumination percentages are computed dynamically from primary datasets, ensuring the tool can drop in future sub-meter LROC/SDEM products seamlessly.
